title: FRM Current Issues, Lesson 8: Cloud provider concentration risk
subtitle: When a whole industry outsources to the same three companies, individual risk becomes systemic risk
whyItMatters: Every institution that moves to the cloud has a good reason: cheaper, safer, faster. But when they all pick one of the same handful of providers, the sum becomes a single point of failure that nobody owns.
openingQuestion: Why do supervisors worry about cloud provider concentration in the financial industry?
openingOptions: One incident can disrupt many institutions at the same moment
Cloud providers usually offer weaker security than self-run systems
Cloud rental costs rise every year and eat into bank profitability
Customer data is legally required to be stored inside national borders
explanation: At the level of a single organisation, cloud infrastructure is usually safer than running your own: a large provider has a security team and a redundancy capability that a mid-sized bank could never build. The problem lives at the system level. When many institutions depend on a handful of providers, one incident produces simultaneous disruption across the whole industry, and no institution can hedge that away with internal measures - which is why supervisors in several countries have begun overseeing the providers directly.

diagram.label: Each organisation moves to the cloud for its own sound reasons
Very few providers are capable enough to serve them
The sum: a shared point of failure for the whole industry
No single institution has any incentive to fix it alone

realWorldExample.company: Why the traditional outsourcing framework is not enough for the cloud
realWorldExample.description: Outsourcing rules were written for a bilateral relationship: the bank assesses the provider, signs a contract with audit clauses, and prepares an alternative. With the cloud all three steps are hard to perform meaningfully - a small bank has no negotiating leverage against a provider many times its size, on-site audit rights are rarely practical, and switching provider is a multi-year programme rather than a contingency option.

quiz.question: Why is the ability to switch provider a practical problem rather than a paper one?
options: Because data held in the cloud cannot technically be copied back out
Because cloud contracts always run ten years with no right to terminate
Because supervisors require each firm to use one provider and no more
Because systems are built on the provider's own services and stick to them
quiz.explanation: The more platform-specific services an application uses, the harder it becomes to detach. This is why a paper contingency plan - if something goes wrong we will move to another provider - is usually impossible to verify in practice. Data can be exported; the obstacle is the surrounding machinery, not the bytes. Contract terms vary widely and are negotiable, and no supervisor mandates single sourcing, which would make the concentration problem worse rather than better.

quiz.question: Why is this classified as systemic risk rather than the operational risk of one bank?
options: Because the outage hits many institutions at once, so none can absorb another's load
Because cloud providers also hold equity stakes in the largest banks
Because a cloud incident always lasts more than a week before being fixed
Because financial data placed in the cloud is shared between the institutions using it
quiz.explanation: Ordinary operational risk is idiosyncratic: if this bank goes down, customers move to another one. When the whole industry runs on shared infrastructure, the incident lands on everyone simultaneously and that natural offsetting mechanism disappears. Cross-shareholdings would be a governance issue rather than a contagion channel, outage duration varies enormously and short outages are still systemic, and a shared provider does not mean shared data.

quiz.question: What direction are supervisors in several countries taking with this risk?
options: Banning financial institutions from using any cloud computing service at all
Supervising critical providers directly instead of only through the banks
Requiring every bank to build and run its own private data centre
Forcing cloud providers to apply for a full banking licence to operate
quiz.explanation: Since no individual institution has the leverage or the incentive to address this shared risk, the trend is to bring critical providers into direct supervision - much the way financial market infrastructures are supervised. An outright ban would push banks back onto weaker infrastructure, mandating private data centres would do the same at greater cost, and a banking licence regulates capital and deposit-taking, which has nothing to do with the operational dependency in question.

quiz.question: Why is moving to a different cloud provider hard in practice?
options: Because data held in the cloud may not legally leave the original provider
Because cloud contracts normally carry a ten-year minimum term
Because the system clings to the provider's proprietary services
Because supervisors must re-approve the entire system after every move
quiz.explanation: A modern application does not merely rent servers - it uses the platform's own database, message queue and identity services. Moving means rewriting most of the system, which is why a paper contingency plan usually cannot be executed in a crisis. There is no general legal bar on moving data out, contract lengths are negotiated and far shorter than a decade, and supervisory approval is a formality compared with the engineering work.

quiz.question: What direction are supervisors in several countries taking with this particular risk?
options: Forcing cloud providers to obtain a banking licence before serving banks
Banning financial institutions from moving core systems onto cloud infrastructure
Requiring every bank to run at least three providers in parallel at all times
Supervising the critical providers themselves rather than only the banks
quiz.explanation: No bank can hedge this risk away with internal measures, so the old framework - placing every obligation on the individual institution - cannot solve it. The route being taken is to bring the provider itself into scope once it becomes important enough to the system. A banking licence addresses the wrong subject matter, a ban on core migration would leave banks on weaker infrastructure, and forcing triple redundancy would multiply cost while barely reducing the shared exposure.

practicePrompt.question: Twelve large banks in one country all pick the same cloud provider, and each of them has done very thorough due diligence on that provider. Where is the problem?
options: Every decision is sound; the sum is a shared point of failure
All twelve due diligence exercises missed the same weakness
That provider carries higher operational risk than its competitors do
Their outsourcing contracts lack a proper exit clause
practicePrompt.explanation: This is the fallacy of composition in its cleanest form: each bank picks the provider with the best infrastructure and the most thorough due diligence, and precisely because they all did the right thing, they all picked the same one. The resulting risk is not contained in any single decision and nobody owns it - no bank can fix it alone, because the only party that sees the whole picture is the supervisor. The traditional outsourcing framework cannot reach it either, because it assumes a bilateral relationship in which the customer has bargaining power, and here the customer is many times smaller than the provider.

keyTakeaways: Sound at the level of each organisation, yet a shared point of failure at the level of the system
The traditional outsourcing framework assumes a balanced bilateral relationship, which does not hold here
The ability to switch provider usually exists only on paper
The regulatory trend: direct supervision of critical providers

summary.keyIdea: This is the clearest example of the fallacy of composition: every individual decision is right, and the sum is a risk nobody owns
summary.commonMistake: Assessing cloud risk only at the level of the organisation, where the conclusion is almost always that it is safer than self-hosting
summary.action: When reviewing third-party risk, add one question: how many of our competitors are using this exact same provider

application.title: Spotting hidden concentration
application.message: Try listing the digital services you use every day, then look up whose infrastructure they run on. The list is usually far shorter than the number of applications.
application.secondary: That is the shape of the concentration risk the whole financial industry is facing.

sections.text: Ask each bank separately and moving to the cloud almost always lowers its operational risk. The hard question only appears when you add all the answers together.

Very few providers are capable of serving large financial institutions. When most of the industry picks from that small group, an incident at one provider is no longer one organisation's incident - it is a simultaneous disruption across many organisations, at exactly the moment nobody is in a normal enough state to cover for anyone else.

items: Asymmetric bargaining power: a small bank cannot impose terms on a provider far larger than itself
On-site audit rights are rarely practical against the cloud operating model
Switching ability is locked in by platform-specific services
Multi-layer dependency chains: the providers' own providers may overlap too

sections.label: Why the market cannot solve this itself
sections.text: No individual institution has any incentive to bear the cost of diversifying infrastructure in order to reduce a risk the whole industry shares. This is a textbook externality, and it is why the answer has to come from regulation rather than from the market.
The fallacy of composition, stated briefly

Ask each bank separately: moving systems to the cloud almost always lowers its operational risk. A large provider has a security team, redundant infrastructure and a patching cadence that a self-run data centre struggles to match. Ask the industry: when most institutions pick from three providers, a single incident touches all of them at once. Both answers are correct, and that is precisely the paradox - optimising each part does not add up to an optimum for the whole.

sections.label: Why the market cannot solve this itself
sections.text: No individual institution has any incentive to bear the cost of diversifying infrastructure in order to reduce a risk the whole industry shares. If one bank runs two platforms in parallel, it pays twice over while the systemic share of the risk falls by almost nothing - because when the large provider goes down, its customers and counterparties are paralysed anyway. This is a textbook externality, and it can only be handled at the level of regulation rather than at the level of a contract.

sections.title: Three things regulation now demands, and why each one
sections.subtitle: All three are answers to the fact that a bilateral contract is not enough

concepts.def: Supervisors have to know who depends on whom before an incident happens. Without that map, the industry's level of concentration is something nobody can measure, even if every individual contract is watertight.

You have to be able to show that if the provider stops serving you, moving is possible, how long it takes, and where to. A small bank's bargaining power against a much larger provider is weak, so a paper clause is no substitute for a plan that has actually been tested.

In practice these are usually replaced by a certification report shared across every customer. That is acceptable for most services, but it means the bank is relying on another third party's assessment rather than checking for itself.

lines: Outsourcing moves the activity, but it does not move the accountability - and here it does not move the risk either.
Next lesson: a recent episode of banking instability and what it confirmed.
